title: Reduced total quotient rings under extension of the ground field
statement:
Let $k$ be a field and $A$ a commutative integral domain (a nonzero commutative ring without zero divisors) that is a finite type $k$-algebra [def-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra]. Write $F=\operatorname{Frac}(A)$ for the localization of $A$ at its nonzero elements [def-weil-pbc-module-localization]. For a field extension $L/k$ [def-pc-field-extension], put $B_L=A\otimes_k L$ [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product], $R_L=B_L/\sqrt{(0)}$, where $\sqrt{(0)}$ is the ideal of nilpotent elements, and $Q_L=S_L^{-1}R_L$, where $S_L$ is the multiplicative set of nonzerodivisors (elements $s$ for which $sx=0$ implies $x=0$). For every tower $k\subseteq L\subseteq M$, the natural map $R_L\to R_M$ is injective and sends nonzerodivisors to nonzerodivisors. It therefore induces an injective map $Q_L\to Q_M$, sending $c/d$ to the fraction of its images. There is a canonical map
$$\theta_L:F\otimes_k L\longrightarrow Q_L,\qquad (a/s)\otimes\lambda\longmapsto\frac{a\otimes\lambda}{s\otimes1},$$
whose kernel is exactly the ideal of nilpotent elements of $F\otimes_k L$. These maps commute with towers of extension fields and with principal localization $A\to A[1/a]$ for every nonzero $a\in A$ (under the resulting canonical identifications of the total quotient rings).

proof.text: For each field extension $L/k$ write $B_L=A\otimes_kL$ and $R_L=B_L/\sqrt{(0)}$.  For a tower $L\subseteq M$, the map $B_L\to B_M$ is the scalar-extension map.  It is injective: choose an $L$-basis of the nonzero $L$-vector space $M$ containing $1$, and the coefficient functional sending $1$ to $1$ gives a retraction of $b\mapsto b\otimes1$.  It is flat: $M$ is a flat $L$-module [lem-weil-pbc-module-over-field-flat], and under the associativity identification $B_M=A\otimes_kM\cong B_L\otimes_LM$ the map $B_L\to B_M$ is $b\mapsto b\otimes1$, so $B_M$ is a flat $B_L$-module by base change of flat modules [lem-weil-pbc-flat-module-base-change].  If the image of $b\in B_L$ is nilpotent, injectivity makes $b$ nilpotent, so the scalar map descends to an injective $R_L\to R_M$.  If a minimal prime of $B_M$ contracts to $\mathfrak p\subset B_L$, then $\mathfrak p$ is minimal: a strictly smaller prime would lift by going down to a strictly smaller prime inside the chosen minimal prime.  Minimal primes are unchanged by passage to the nilradical quotients.  Hence a nonzerodivisor of $R_L$, which lies in no minimal prime by the reduced-ring zerodivisor theorem, maps to an element lying in no minimal prime of $R_M$, and is therefore a nonzerodivisor there.

source.place: Tag 0C3N, second proof paragraph: scalar extension, the canonical map of reduced rings, and the nonzerodivisor/minimal-prime argument

proof.text: The injective map $R_L\to R_M$ sends the multiplicative set $S_L$ of nonzerodivisors into $S_M$.  The universal property of localization therefore gives $Q_L=S_L^{-1}R_L\to Q_M=S_M^{-1}R_M$, with $c/d\mapsto\bar c/\bar d$.  If a fraction maps to zero, some nonzerodivisor of $R_M$ annihilates the image of its numerator; that nonzerodivisor forces the image numerator to be zero, and injectivity of $R_L\to R_M$ forces the numerator itself to be zero.  Thus the induced map $Q_L\to Q_M$ is injective.

source.place: Tag 0C3N, second proof paragraph: canonical map between total rings of fractions

proof.text:
For $s\in A\setminus\{0\}$, multiplication by $s$ on the domain $A$ is injective.  After tensoring with the field $L$ it remains injective (the same basis argument as above), so $s\otimes1$ is a nonzerodivisor in $B_L$.  Its image is still a nonzerodivisor in $R_L$: if $(s\otimes1)b$ is nilpotent, then a power of $s\otimes1$ kills a power of $b$, and injectivity of multiplication by that power gives that $b$ is nilpotent.  Define $\beta:F\times L\to Q_L$ by $\beta(a/s,\lambda)=(a\otimes\lambda)/(s\otimes1)$. It is well defined: if $a/s=a'/s'$ in $F$ then $as'=a's$ in the domain $A$, so $(a\otimes\lambda)(s'\otimes1)=(a'\otimes\lambda)(s\otimes1)$ and the two fractions agree in $Q_L$. It is $k$-bilinear (bring two fractions to the common denominator $ss'$). The universal property of the tensor product gives the $k$-linear map $\theta_L:F\otimes_kL\to Q_L$ with
$$\theta_L((a/s)\otimes\lambda)=(a\otimes\lambda)/(s\otimes1),$$
and checking on pure tensors shows that $\theta_L$ is a ring homomorphism, that it restricts on the image of $B_L$ to $B_L\to R_L\to Q_L$, and that $\theta_L((1/s)z)=(s\otimes1)^{-1}\theta_L(z)$ for the $F$-module structure of $F\otimes_kL$.

source.place: Tag 0C3N, second proof paragraph: canonical fraction map from $Q(A_{red})\otimes_kL$ to $Q((A\otimes_kL)_{red})$

proof.text: Every element of $F\otimes_kL$ can be written, after bringing finitely many pure tensors $(a_i/s_i)\otimes\lambda_i$ to a common denominator $s=\prod s_i$, as $b/s:=(1/s)\cdot\iota(b)$ with $b\in B_L$, $s\in A\setminus\{0\}$ and $\iota:B_L\to F\otimes_kL$ the map $a\otimes\lambda\mapsto(a/1)\otimes\lambda$. By step 3, $\theta_L(b/s)=(s\otimes1)^{-1}\bar b/1$.  If $\theta_L(b/s)=0$, the localization zero criterion gives a nonzerodivisor $t\in R_L$ with $t\bar b=0$.  Since $t$ is a nonzerodivisor, $\bar b=0$, so $b$ is nilpotent in $B_L$ and $b/s$ is nilpotent in $F\otimes_kL$.  Conversely, $Q_L$ is a localization of the reduced ring $R_L$, hence is reduced; a nilpotent element of $F\otimes_kL$ therefore maps to zero.  Thus $\ker\theta_L$ is exactly the nilpotent ideal.

source.place: Tag 0C3N, second proof paragraph: the kernel consists of nilpotent elements

proof.text: All constructions above are induced by the structural tensor maps, quotient-to-the-reduction maps, and localization maps.  On pure tensors and represented fractions they send an element to the fraction of its image.  Associativity of tensor products gives equality for a tower $k\subseteq L\subseteq M$, and the localization universal property gives equality after replacing $A$ by $A[1/a]$ for any nonzero $a\in A$.  These equalities agree on overlaps and hence are the asserted canonical tower and principal-localization compatibilities.
